blocks.text: Common station instructions include:
“Take a focused history from a 62-year-old woman with postmenopausal bleeding.”
“A vaginal lesion has been found on speculum examination. Describe your examination and investigations.”
“Discuss the diagnosis and management of a biopsy-confirmed vaginal squamous cell carcinoma.”

items: “Counsel a patient who has been diagnosed with vaginal cancer.”
“Interpret a pelvic MRI and discuss the likely stage.”

blocks.text: Vaginal cancer is a malignant tumour arising from the vagina. It is distinct from cervical cancer, although the two can have similar risk factors and may coexist with other lower genital tract lesions.
The most common primary vaginal malignancy. It is often associated with persistent high-risk HPV infection and usually affects older women.
Less common. Certain clear cell adenocarcinomas have an association with in-utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES), although this is rare in contemporary practice.
These include vaginal melanoma, sarcoma and other uncommon histological types.
This distinction is important in clinical practice.
Primary vaginal cancer: originates in the vagina.
Secondary involvement: cancer has spread to the vagina from the cervix, vulva, endometrium, bladder, rectum or another site.
A lesion in the vagina is not automatically a primary vaginal cancer.

rows: Most primary vaginal cancers occur in older women
Important in vaginal squamous cell carcinoma
Indicates increased risk of related lower genital tract disease

Associated with HPV-related lower genital tract malignancies

blocks.text: HPV vaccination and appropriate cervical screening can reduce the burden of HPV-associated disease, but neither eliminates the possibility of vaginal cancer.
Postmenopausal bleeding.
Intermenstrual bleeding.
Bleeding after sexual intercourse.
Persistent watery, blood-stained or foul-smelling vaginal discharge.
Pelvic or vaginal pain.
Pain during intercourse.
A vaginal lump or sensation of a mass.
Dysuria or urinary frequency.
Constipation or rectal symptoms if adjacent structures are involved.
Some women are asymptomatic, with a lesion identified during examination.
A bulky vaginal mass.
Persistent pelvic pain.
Haematuria or rectal bleeding due to possible local invasion or another primary tumour.
Urinary obstruction or hydronephrosis.
Rectovaginal or vesicovaginal fistula.
Enlarged inguinal or pelvic lymph nodes, depending on tumour location.
Exam tip: Postmenopausal bleeding must be investigated even when the amount of bleeding is small or intermittent.
Introduce yourself and confirm the patient's identity.
Explain that you would like to ask about her symptoms and relevant medical history.
Obtain consent and ensure privacy.
Offer a chaperone for any intimate examination.
Ask about her immediate concerns.
When did the bleeding begin?
Is it spontaneous, after intercourse or after urination?
How much blood is present?
Is it associated with pain?
Has it occurred after menopause?
Is the discharge watery, blood-stained or foul-smelling?
How long has it been present?
Is there associated itching or pain?
Is the pain vaginal, pelvic or abdominal?
Is it constant or intermittent?
Does intercourse cause pain?
Is there pain on passing urine or stool?
Have you noticed a lump or a feeling of something protruding?
Any urinary frequency, difficulty passing urine or constipation?
Any unexplained weight loss or fatigue?
Ask about:
Menstrual and menopausal status.
Obstetric history and vaginal deliveries.
Previous cervical screening results.
HPV-related disease, genital warts or abnormal cervical cytology.
Previous cervical, vulval, endometrial or vaginal cancer.
Previous pelvic radiotherapy or surgery.
Hormonal medication and any relevant history of DES exposure.
HIV or other immunosuppression, where relevant.
Previous malignancies and their treatment.
Current medication, allergies and comorbidities.
Smoking history.
Impact of symptoms on sexual function, relationships and daily activities.
Patient concerns and available support.
Use sensitive, non-judgemental language when asking about sexual history and HPV-associated conditions.
Explain the examination, obtain consent and provide a chaperone. Ensure privacy, appropriate exposure and good lighting.
Assess:
General condition, pallor and weight loss.
Vital signs.
Abdominal masses or tenderness.
Supraclavicular and inguinal lymph nodes where appropriate.
Peripheral oedema or other evidence of advanced disease.
Inspect and palpate for:
Abdominal distension.
Pelvic or abdominal masses.
Tenderness.
Ascites.
Organomegaly, where relevant.
Inspect the vagina systematically, including the anterior and posterior walls, lateral walls, fornices and cervix.
Describe any lesion by:
Site: upper, middle or lower third; anterior, posterior or lateral wall.
Size: measured in centimetres.
Number: solitary or multiple.
Surface: smooth, ulcerated, irregular, friable or fungating.
Margins: regular or irregular.
Bleeding: spontaneous or on contact.
Discharge: present or absent.
Extension: whether the cervix or vulva is involved or appears to be the primary site.
If the lesion is friable, avoid unnecessary manipulation.
Assess:
Vaginal wall thickening or induration.
Tumour mobility and fixation.
Cervical involvement.
Pelvic tenderness or masses.
When indicated and with consent, assess:
Posterior vaginal wall involvement.
Rectal involvement.
Parametrial or paravaginal induration.
The relationship of the lesion to adjacent pelvic structures.

Assess pelvic and inguinal nodes as clinically indicated. Lymphatic drainage depends partly on tumour location: upper vaginal lesions more commonly drain to pelvic nodes, while lower vaginal lesions may involve inguinal nodes.

“On speculum examination, the vaginal walls appear healthy with no visible ulceration, mass or abnormal discharge. The cervix appears normal. Bimanual examination reveals no palpable vaginal wall thickening or pelvic mass.”

“Speculum examination reveals a 3 cm irregular, friable ulcerated lesion on the upper posterior vaginal wall, which bleeds on contact. The cervix appears separate from the lesion. Bimanual examination suggests local induration. These findings are suspicious for vaginal malignancy, although histology is required to confirm the diagnosis and determine whether the lesion is primary or secondary.”
A biopsy of the suspicious vaginal lesion is essential to establish histology.
It helps determine:
Malignant versus benign pathology.
Histological subtype.
Tumour grade and invasion.
Whether the lesion may represent secondary involvement from another primary tumour.
A biopsy should be planned carefully, especially if the lesion is highly vascular or near the urethra, bladder or rectum.

blocks.text: This is a high-yield exam point. Before diagnosing primary vaginal cancer, assess for:
Cervical cancer extending into the vagina.
Vulval cancer extending proximally.
Endometrial cancer involving the vagina.
Bladder or colorectal malignancy involving the vaginal wall.
Recurrence of a previous gynaecological cancer.
The required assessment depends on the lesion's location, histology, symptoms and prior medical history.

rows: Cervical lesion, abnormal cervical cytology or biopsy, possible vaginal extension
Postmenopausal bleeding, endometrial abnormality or uterine pathology
Previous malignancy or evidence of another primary site
Often smooth and non-ulcerated, but suspicious lesions still require assessment
Discharge, erythema or irritation without a persistent malignant-appearing mass
Relevant history and an appropriate lesion pattern
Bulging related to pelvic organ support rather than a discrete ulcerated mass

blocks.text: Vaginal cancer is staged according to the extent of local disease and spread.

rows: Disease confined to the vaginal wall
Extension into paravaginal tissues but not to the pelvic wall
Involvement of the bladder or rectal mucosa, or extension beyond the true pelvis or distant spread, according to FIGO criteria

blocks.text: Important distinction: Extension to nearby structures does not always mean stage IV. The precise stage depends on the anatomical criteria and the current staging system. Histology and imaging must be reviewed together.
Management depends on histology, tumour site, stage, previous treatment and the patient's general condition. It should be planned by a specialist MDT.
Selected small, localised tumours may be treated with:
Surgery in carefully selected patients.
Radiotherapy, including brachytherapy where appropriate.
A combination of external-beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy, depending on the tumour and treatment plan.
Surgery is not automatically the best option for every early vaginal cancer because the anatomy and proximity to the bladder, urethra and rectum can make surgery morbid.
Radiotherapy is central to the management of many vaginal squamous cell carcinomas.
Treatment may include:
External-beam radiotherapy.
Intracavitary or interstitial brachytherapy.
Concurrent chemotherapy, often cisplatin-based in eligible patients, depending on the clinical scenario and local protocol.
Depending on the extent and previous treatment:
Systemic therapy may be considered.
Surgery may be appropriate for selected local recurrences.
Radiotherapy may be used if not previously delivered or if retreatment is feasible.
Symptom-directed treatment and palliative care may be appropriate.
Address:
Pain and bleeding.
Anaemia and nutritional status.
Urinary or bowel symptoms.
Sexual health and vaginal changes following treatment.
Menopausal symptoms, fertility implications and psychological distress.
Vaginal dilators, lubricants, moisturisers and psychosexual support may be useful after treatment in selected patients, guided by the treating team.
Possible complications of vaginal cancer itself include:
Persistent bleeding and anaemia.
Pain and discharge.
Urinary obstruction.
Rectal involvement or fistula formation.
Local invasion and distant spread.
Potential treatment-related complications include:
Vaginal dryness, stenosis or shortening.
Dyspareunia.
Bladder or bowel irritation after radiotherapy.
Infertility or ovarian dysfunction, depending on treatment exposure.
Surgical complications and effects on sexual function.
These risks should be discussed individually, without assuming that every patient will experience them.

subsections.subsection_title: Counselling a patient with suspected vaginal cancer

blocks.text: Ask what the patient understands about the abnormal finding.
Explain that the lesion requires further investigation and that its appearance alone cannot confirm cancer.
Explain the biopsy procedure and why tissue diagnosis is important.
Discuss the possible need for MRI or other imaging.
Explain that treatment depends on the histology, stage and location.
Ask about concerns related to fertility, sexual function, relationships and body image.
Offer emotional support and an opportunity to ask questions.
Confirm the referral and follow-up plan.

“The examination has identified an area that we need to investigate further. There are several possible causes, but because the area looks abnormal, we need to take a small tissue sample and examine it under a microscope. We may also arrange imaging to understand its extent. If the biopsy confirms cancer, the specialist team will explain the treatment options based on the type and location of the tumour. I appreciate that this can be worrying, and we will support you through the investigations and decisions.”
Q1. What is the most common histological type of vaginal cancer?
Squamous cell carcinoma.
Q2. What is the most important investigation?
Biopsy of the suspicious lesion for histological confirmation.
Q3. Why must you exclude cervical cancer?
Cervical cancer can extend into the vagina. A vaginal lesion may therefore represent direct extension or recurrence rather than a primary vaginal malignancy.
Q4. What are the major risk factors?
Persistent high-risk HPV infection, increasing age, immunosuppression, smoking and a history of lower genital tract precancer or cancer.
Q5. What is the role of MRI?
MRI helps assess local tumour extent and its relationship to adjacent structures, which assists staging and treatment planning.
Q6. What is the role of radiotherapy?
Radiotherapy, often combined with brachytherapy, is a major treatment modality for many vaginal cancers. Concurrent chemotherapy may be used in selected patients.
Q7. Does cervical screening diagnose vaginal cancer?
No. Cervical screening primarily assesses risk of cervical precancer and cancer. A suspicious vaginal lesion needs direct clinical assessment and biopsy.
Q8. What symptoms may indicate advanced local disease?
Urinary obstruction, haematuria, rectal symptoms, fistula formation, severe pelvic pain or evidence of adjacent-organ involvement.
Q9. Why is tumour location important?
It influences the structures at risk, lymphatic drainage, staging and the feasibility of surgery or radiotherapy.
Q10. What is the importance of sexual health counselling?
Cancer and treatment may affect vaginal function, intimacy, body image and relationships. These concerns should be discussed sensitively, with appropriate rehabilitation and psychological support.

“This patient presents with persistent vaginal bleeding. Speculum examination reveals an irregular ulcerated lesion on the upper vaginal wall, with contact bleeding. The cervix appears separate from the lesion. I would assess the lesion's size and extent, examine the vulva and cervix, and perform appropriate pelvic and lymph-node examinations.

“My main differential diagnosis is vaginal malignancy. Other possibilities include cervical cancer with vaginal extension, endometrial cancer involving the vagina and a benign vaginal lesion. I would arrange biopsy for histological confirmation, appropriate imaging and specialist gynaecological oncology assessment.”
Assuming that every vaginal lesion is a primary vaginal cancer.
Forgetting to examine the cervix and vulva.
Treating persistent bleeding as benign without assessment.
Relying on imaging without histological confirmation.
Failing to assess possible bladder or rectal involvement.
Discussing treatment without considering tumour site, stage and patient preferences.

A 66-year-old woman presents with persistent vaginal bleeding. Speculum examination shows an ulcerated lesion on the upper vaginal wall, while the cervix appears normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

items: A. Diagnose primary vaginal cancer from the appearance alone
B. Prescribe vaginal oestrogen and review in one year

blocks.text: C. Arrange biopsy and investigate whether the lesion is primary or secondary
V — Vaginal bleeding or persistent discharge.
A — Assess the cervix, vulva and adjacent structures.
G — Get a biopsy for histological diagnosis.
I — Image to assess local and distant extent when indicated.
N — Note the lymphatic drainage and nodal status.
